name: Marathi
confidence_why: Pandharipande 1997 (the Routledge reference grammar), Dhongde & Wali 2009 and the acoustic study of Le Grezause 2016 all describe Marathi stress as weight-sensitive with the leftmost syllable stressed when weights are equal; the only dissent is old (Joshi 1900 puts the default on the penult, and Bloch 1914 doubted that Marathi has an intensity accent at all), while Pandharipande's own warning that her rules are tentative is what the record's hedge already carries.

sweep_summary: Marathi (mara1378, catalog: weight-hedged on Pandharipande 1997 sec. 3.3.2 with Dhongde & Wali 2009 secondary). the list of works with stress in the title holds one Glottolog title hit, Auchlin 2013 'Prosodic iconicity and experiential blending' (Benjamins): a general theory chapter with no Marathi content; Glottolog's own record says the Marathi link is a computerized assignment from the word 'blending'. Not relevant, priority none. Beyond the list, open first-hand sources downloaded and read into Joshi 1900 grammar secs. 176-185 (penultimate default; final if it ends in a long vowel; accented vowel long; conjunct-final keeps short penult accented) refines the catalog's weight rule with a penultimate default; Bloch 1914 secs. 32-36 (with the 1970 English translation) surveys Joshi vs Navalkar and judges an intensity accent unproven, confirming the hedge; Grierson 1905 LSI vol. VII has accent remarks only for Konkani dialects. Le Grezause 2016 JASA abstract (already held by the project) confirms weight-sensitive stress with CVX heavy and first-syllable default for disyllables; its full poster/manuscript remains unlocated and is the top acquisition priority. No source read supersedes Pandharipande 1997; catalog's classification stands. DuckDuckGo HTML fallback timed out; Benjamins and pubs.aip.org landing pages could not be reached by automated download.

new_statements.reading: A native grammarian's first-hand (1900) statement: default penultimate stress, shifted to a final long vowel; the stressed vowel is long (or lengthened), and a word-final conjunct keeps the stress on a short penult. That is a weight-sensitive system with a penultimate default rather than Pandharipande 1997's position-free 'leftmost heavy / initial default' rules; the two agree on disyllables (initial unless only the final is heavy) and diverge on trisyllables. Bloch 1914 secs. 34-36 (also read) reports Joshi's penultimate rule beside Navalkar's 'initial syllable slightly raised' and concludes that an intensity accent is unproven for Marathi, which supports keeping the catalog's hedge. scanned caveats: 'Accent' prints as 'Aooent'; the Devanagari vowel letters in sec. 179 are garbled in the text, so the bracketed vowels are inferred from context.

new_statements.rule_in_words: Stress is non-distinctive and weak. Syllable weight decides: CV light, CVV and CVC heavy, CVVC superheavy; [i:], [u:], [a:], [e], [o] count as long vowels, [a], [i], [u] as short. A word with a single heavy or superheavy syllable stresses it wherever it stands. Disyllables with two heavies or two lights stress the first. Trisyllables: all heavy or first two heavy -> first syllable; second and third heavy -> second; only the last heavy -> last; only the middle heavy -> middle. No all-light trisyllables exist. The same rules hold for nouns and verbs. Marathi has no tones and pitch is not distinctive (3.3.3, p. 559); stress and tonal structure are not affected by morphological processes (3.5, p. 576).
new_statements.secondary_stress: Not discussed; only 'the locus of the main/primary stress' is marked in the examples (p. 556). The bold/underlined stress marks on the examples are lost in the scanned text (they surface as '&', '4', '@'), so the example placements are not verified here; the prose rules are.
new_statements.exceptions: None stated; the author flags the whole account as 'tentative' and stress as 'one of the least investigated areas of Marathi phonology' (p. 555).

readall_conflicts: The only source newly read (Pandharipande 1997, standing in for the unobtainable 2003 chapter) and the existing Joshi 1900 statement are both weight-sensitive and both say the stressed syllable is the heavy one when there is only one, but their defaults differ when several syllables are heavy: Pandharipande stresses the leftmost heavy (first syllable in all-heavy and first-two-heavy trisyllables; second syllable only when the second and third alone are heavy), whereas Joshi's rule is penultimate unless the final has a long vowel, giving the penult in all-heavy trisyllables. They agree on every disyllable and on trisyllables with one heavy syllable or with heavy second+third. Pandharipande also states outright that stress is 'not distinctive' and 'not a prominent feature', and calls her own rules tentative; Bloch 1914 (already on record) doubted that an intensity accent was proven at all. So the placement is weight-driven in every source, but the direction of the default (initial vs penultimate) among heavy syllables is contested and no source claims contrastive stress.

sources.quote: 176. Accent is the stress upon some particular syllable of a word. Every Marathi word consisting of more than one syllable has its accent; i. e., a stress is laid on one of its syllables. 177. It is a general rule in Marathi, that when there are two or three syllables in a word, the penultimate syllable is accented (see Ch. I. XXI). 178. When a word consists of more than three syllables, the syllables accented are generally more than one. But the penultimate letter of every Marathi word is generally accented. 179. When a word ends in [ī] or in a long [ū] or [ā] the last syllable is accented although the penultimate syllable has a long vowel.
sources.locator: Part III 'Accent' secs. 176-185 (djvu lines 8354-8420); Ch. I sec. XXI (lines 1537-1547)
sources.note: First-hand 1900 grammarian statement: penultimate stress as the general rule; final stress when the word ends in a long vowel (historically the old penultimate); the accented vowel is 'always long'; a word ending in a conjunct consonant keeps penultimate accent even with a short vowel (sec. 181); a prosodically long antepenult may take the accent, 'but such words may as well follow the general rule' (sec. 184). scanned: 'Accent' printed 'Aooent'; Devanagari vowel letters in sec. 179 are garbled in the text (bracketed vowels are my reading of the context, not verbatim).
